cryo_bay_breached.trigger: Flip to true when a cryo pod is physically opened or damaged, exposing a colonist host to the outbreak or the parasite to the ship at large.

adventure_complete.trigger: Flip to true when the player either seals the parasite outbreak and stabilizes the hull long enough to reach the relay beacon, OR the ship is lost/abandoned (escape pods launched or player character dies), resolving the central survival arc.

mara_found_the_logs.trigger: Flip to true when the player or Mara physically accesses the falsified maintenance logs in the engineering records terminal.

hull_cascade_triggered.trigger: Flip to true when a structural stress event (explosion, collision, or deliberate sabotage) initiates the first breach in the cascade sequence.

insurance_scam_exposed.trigger: Flip to true when Mara (or the player) connects the falsified logs to the insurance payout structure and confronts the captain or transmits the evidence off-ship.

parasite_outbreak_known.trigger: Flip to true when a crew member or the player directly witnesses a host exhibiting motor-control loss and identifies it as infection rather than illness or injury.

mara_becomes_threat_to_captain.trigger: Flip to true when insurance_scam_exposed is true and Mara moves to act on the evidence — confronting, sabotaging, or transmitting.

worldFacts.ship_layout: The Halbrecht is a long colony transport with three decks linked by a single central ladder shaft. Upper deck: bridge, comms array, captain's quarters, engineering records terminal (aft of bridge). Mid deck: crew berths, mess hall, medbay, and the cryo bay (a vast, cold chamber holding hundreds of pods, accessible only from mid-deck via a heavy blast door). Lower deck: cargo bay, engine room, life support processing, and the aft airlock. The ladder shaft is the only fast route between decks; it is narrow, poorly lit, and prone to sudden pressure differentials during hull stress events. The engine room and life support processing sit adjacent to a section of hull already showing stress fractures — the likely origin point of any breach cascade.
worldFacts.colonist_count: 412 colonists in cryo suspension across the mid-deck cryo bay, tended automatically; active crew numbers six including Danny and Mara.
worldFacts.danny_relationship: Danny and Mara shipped together before; he half-trusts her paranoia about corporate malfeasance but has no direct stake in her crusade — yet.
worldFacts.communications_status: Long-range comms are down for repairs the captain claims were 'scheduled'; the nearest relay beacon is three weeks out at current burn.
worldFacts.cryo_bay_bulkhead_patch: Danny has sealant-taped the visible stress fractures along the cryo bay bulkhead weld seam using standard patch kits. Cosmetic/temporary — unknown whether it addresses underlying structural fatigue. The vibration in the plating persists.
worldFacts.crew_roster: Six active crew: Captain Voss (bridge, likely complicit or blame-bearer), First Mate Okonkwo-Reyes (bridge, comms/nav, currently running diagnostics since long-range comms are down), Chief Engineer Petrov (lower deck, engine room/life support — plausibly aware of true hull condition), Danny and Mara (cargo handlers), Teo (other cargo hand, keeps to himself, bunks near mess).
worldFacts.insurance_file_copies: The falsified maintenance logs / insurance schedule evidence now exists on two slates: Mara's and Danny's, copied as a redundancy in case either is seized or destroyed.
worldFacts.crew_awareness_status: Danny and Mara have confirmed insurance hazard-multiplier file contents together. Plan: Danny briefs Teo (cargo hand) and confronts Petrov (chief engineer) with him as backup. Mara stays topside watching Voss for pod activity or contact with Okonkwo-Reyes. Danny is to signal Mara before confronting Petrov.
worldFacts.teo_awareness_status: Teo has been briefed by Danny on both the backdated hull certification and the insurance hazard-multiplier clause. He held composure (no Panic) but is visibly shaken and has committed to confronting Petrov alongside Danny. He wants a signal sent to Mara before the confrontation happens.

narrative.location: The colony transport ESV Halbrecht, three weeks out from the nearest relay beacon, running on a skeleton crew of six while four hundred and twelve colonists sleep in cryo. The ship is old, its maintenance logs falsified, and its bones are tired.
narrative.atmosphere: Cold, dim, and too quiet. Emergency lighting has replaced half the fixtures because the main grid keeps browning out. The recycled air tastes metallic. Every groan of the hull sounds like it could be the last one. There is no one to call for help and everyone aboard knows it.

npcAgendas.danny: Teamster hauling freight and half-listening to Mara's paranoia until the ship starts proving her right.
npcAgendas.mara_odinsen: Has now confirmed via decrypted insurance schedule that the Halbrecht's insured value scales with crew/colonist casualties -- a designed loss, not mere neglect. Has redundant copies of evidence on both her and Danny's slates. Now wants eyes on Captain Voss (escape pod activity, contact with Okonkwo-Reyes) while Danny brings Teo in and confronts Petrov, the chief engineer, about the ship's true condition. Trusts Danny completely, still feels time is short, wants confirmation of who's complicit before deciding whether to confront the captain directly, sabotage, or transmit evidence off-ship.

narrative.hiddenTruth: The Halbrecht is insured for far more than it's worth operational, and the company quietly greenlit this run knowing the hull would likely fail catastrophically before reaching the colony site — a designed loss, with hazard-multiplier payouts for crew and colonist casualties baked into the actuarial math. The parasitic organism loose in the cryo bay was a known risk the company chose not to disclose, because losing colonists to infection only sweetens the claim.
narrative.oracleConnections: The union enforcer Mara is the one person aboard positioned to notice the mission itself violates labor law and hazard-clause obligations — if she connects the falsified maintenance logs to the insurance payout structure, she becomes a direct political threat to whoever aboard is complicit in the scam. The parasitic organism, discovered among the cryo pods, represents the company's foreknowledge made flesh: hundreds of immobile colonists are both a horror and a possible containment strategy. The isolation of deep transit means the hull's structural failures and the parasite's slow spread both have to be handled with no outside help — every choice is final.

gmContextBlob.openingNarration:
The ladder shaft groans as you climb down to mid-deck, a long metallic sigh that seems to come from somewhere deeper than the hull plating should allow. The emergency lights out here run amber instead of white — half the fixtures on this level went dark two nights ago and nobody's fixed them yet. Your breath fogs faintly; environmental's been struggling to keep pace with the cryo bay's draw.

Mara Odinsen is waiting at the bottom of the ladder, arms crossed, a data slate tucked under one elbow like she's been standing there a while. "You seeing this?" she says, not quite a greeting, and taps the bulkhead beside her. A hairline crack runs along the seam, dusted with a faint rime of frost that shouldn't be there — condensation freezing in a gap that shouldn't exist on a ship this age, this maintained. Except it isn't maintained, not really, and you both know the captain's logs say otherwise.

Somewhere above you, the ship groans again, and four hundred and twelve people sleep on, unaware that the sound might be the last warning anyone gets.

messages.content: OOC: What do I know about this ship? About Mara?
OOC: What do I know about this ship? About Mara?

[OOC: Here's what Danny would actually know at this point, no rolls needed — this is just recap/orientation.]

**The ship — ESV Halbrecht:**
You've been aboard three weeks now, hauling freight and doing the unglamorous work of keeping four hundred and twelve colonists asleep while the ship gets them there. She's an old bird. The maintenance logs say she had a full refit before this run, but you've seen the actual state of the conduits in the lower deck, and "full refit" is not the phrase that comes to mind. Emergency lighting's been up on half the mid-deck since day four because the main grid keeps browning out, and nobody's given you a straight answer why. Long-range comms are down too — the captain says it's "scheduled maintenance," which is the kind of thing captains say when they don't want a follow-up question.

Layout-wise: three decks, one central ladder shaft connecting them, narrow and badly lit. Upper deck has the bridge, comms, the captain's quarters, and the engineering records terminal tucked aft of the bridge. Mid-deck is crew berths, the mess, medbay, and the cryo bay — a big cold chamber, blast-door sealed, holding all four hundred-plus colonists. Lower deck is cargo, the engine room, life support, and the aft airlock. You've noticed — because you've had to work near it — that there are stress fractures already visible in the hull plating around the engine room and life support. Nobody's flagged it officially. You have.

Six live crew total, including you and Mara. It's a skeleton run for a ship this size.

**Mara Odinsen:**
You've shipped with her before — she's solid, competent, not someone who spooks easy. She's aboard under a cargo-handler contract, and she's good at the job: trained hands with Zero-G work and general ship's athletics. But since before you even broke orbit, she's had a bad feeling about this run specifically. She doesn't trust the officers — any of them — and she's been quietly building something. You've caught her cross-referencing hazard-pay clauses against the manifest, asking pointed questions about evacuation protocol nobody asked her to ask. She hasn't said outright what she thinks is going on, but you know Mara well enough to know she doesn't do paranoia for sport. If she's circling something, there's usually a reason.

You don't have a stake in whatever she's chasing. Not yet.]
"Yeah, I see it," I say to Mara. "'Full refit,' my ass."

Mara doesn't look at you when she answers — she's got a panel cover off near the ladder shaft junction, running a thumb along a weld seam that's gone the wrong color.

"Full refit," she repeats, flat. "I pulled the work order myself before we broke orbit. Signed off by a yard supervisor whose license lapsed eight months prior. You want to know how I know that? Because I checked. Nobody checks. That's the whole trick." She lets the panel cover hang on its hinge and finally turns to you. "This ship shouldn't have cleared inspection. It cleared inspection. Someone wanted it to."

She jerks her chin toward the ladder shaft, down toward the lower deck. "There's a terminal upstairs, aft of the bridge. Engineering records. If the falsification goes deeper than one lazy signature, it's in there. I've been trying to get five minutes alone with it since we left dock." Her jaw tightens. "Captain doesn't let cargo handlers wander the upper deck unescorted. Wonder why."

She's watching you now, gauging something. "You in, or is this still my problem?"
"I don't like it," I say without committing. "Do we have the equipment to fix this? Might be a higher priority than chasing down the records."

Mara's mouth twists — not quite a smile. "Fix it. Sure." She taps the discolored weld with one knuckle, and it gives off a sound that's wrong, a little too hollow. "We've got patch kits rated for micro-fractures. Sealant foam, some structural tape that's better than nothing. What we don't have is a yard, a drydock, or replacement plating for a hull section that's been flexing wrong for God knows how long. If this is what I think it is — stress fatigue working its way through the frame — we can slow it. We can't fix it. Not out here."

She straightens up, wipes her hand on her coveralls. "And that's the thing that keeps me up, Danny. A patch job buys time. The records terminal tells us whether we're patching a ship that was supposed to make it, or babysitting a hull they already wrote off." She holds your eyes. "Those are different jobs. I'd like to know which one I'm doing before it decides for me."

Down the corridor, the lights flicker once — a half-second brownout, the kind you've both stopped flinching at — and steady again. Neither of you comments on it.

"So," she says. "Patch kit's in the lower deck lockup, by engineering. Terminal's upstairs, past the bridge, and I need someone running interference or a better reason to be up there than 'felt like it.' Pick one. I can't do both alone."
"Sure, I don't mind distracting know-it-all captains," I say with a grin. "Maybe he caught the latest Premier League scores on Risus 7 before we broke orbit."

That gets an actual laugh out of her — short, surprised, like it's been a while since anyone made her do that. "Risus 7. Right. I'm sure the captain's a football man." She's already moving, checking the corridor both ways out of old habit. "Give me ten minutes after you've got him talking. If he's the type to enjoy an audience, that buys me more — don't let him wrap it up early."

She heads for the ladder shaft, then pauses with one boot on the first rung. "And Danny — if the terminal's locked behind something more than a door, I'll signal. Don't come running if it goes loud. Just... know it went loud."

She climbs. You give her the ten minutes, then head for the bridge, working out in your head what a deckhand who's never cared about ship's business before is suddenly curious enough to ask about. The captain's a man who likes being asked things. That much you can use.

The bridge hatch is standing open when you get there — Captain Voss is alone at the nav station, half-lit by the glow of a course-plot he's been staring at longer than a routine check should take. He looks up when your shadow crosses the threshold, and for just a second, before his face resets into something professional, you catch what might be tiredness. Or might be something closer to guilt.

"Hauling something, or did you get lost?" he says.
I want to make small talk with the captain, ask him about football, ask him if he's flown a lot of colony gigs like this, anything to keep him occupied. Is there a roll for that?

No roll needed — this is just conversation, and the price of failure here isn't high, it's just how long you can hold his attention.

You lean against the hatch frame like you've got nowhere else to be. "Lost implies I had somewhere to be in the first place. Nah, just restless. Cryo shift's boring as hell when you're not the one sleeping through it." You nod at the plot on his console without really looking at it. "Hey, you catch anything before we broke orbit? Risus 7 was supposed to have a match going, some derby thing. Half the crew was arguing about it in the mess before launch."

Voss's shoulders come down half an inch — this is easier ground than whatever he was staring at. "Missed it. We shipped out two days early." He says it like it still needles him. "Company moved the window up. Didn't get a reason, just got a new departure time."

"Two days early," you say, keeping it light, just a deckhand making noise. "Must've been a hell of a scramble getting cargo loaded."

"You have no idea." He almost smiles, rubs at his eyes. "You do a lot of these long hauls?"

"First colony run. You?"

"Eleven years," he says, and there's something in how fast that number comes out — not proud, just tired, like he's said it to justify himself before. "This is the biggest ship I've had. Also the oldest." He catches himself, glances back at the plot, and the ease drains out of his face a little. "Anyway. Don't you have a shift?"

He's still talking, but you can feel him starting to want the conversation to end. If you want more time out of him, you'll need to either ask something that hooks his attention again or accept you're on borrowed minutes now.
"11 years is a long time. You ever have the company bump the schedule up on you like that before?"

The question lands somewhere it wasn't supposed to. Voss goes still for just a fraction of a second — not long, but you clock it, the way his hand stops moving on the console.

"Bumped up? Sure. Company does what the company does." He says it too fast, and then seems to hear himself say it too fast, because he adds, "Cargo manifests shift, insurance windows shift, whatever. Eleven years, you stop asking why." He turns back to the plot, and this time it's not idle — he's making a show of being busy. "This one's just... a bigger contract than usual. More eyes on it upstairs."

"Insurance windows," you repeat, like it's a throwaway. "That a thing that moves departure dates?"

He doesn't answer that one. Instead: "You said you had a shift." Not a question this time.

Whatever door was cracked open a second ago, he's closing it. He's not hostile — not yet — but the easy tiredness from a minute ago has hardened into something more careful, more aware of you as a person asking questions rather than a bored deckhand killing time. If Mara needed more minutes, you've bought a few, but you've also put yourself on his radar in a way you weren't before.
I shift my weight to the other foot, "Hey, you got a favorite team back on Risus?"

You let the insurance thread drop like it never mattered, easy as anything, and shift your weight to the other foot. "Hey, you got a favorite team back on Risus?"

It's clumsy — a little too obvious a pivot after where the conversation just was — and Voss's eyes flick to you for a second with something that isn't quite suspicion yet, more like recalibration. Like he's re-filing you from *bored deckhand* to *bored deckhand asking oddly specific questions right before asking about football.*

But he answers. "Kestrel Reach," he says, distracted, already turning half back to his console. "Wife dragged me to a match once, years back. Been stuck with them since." He taps something on the plot, closes a window that was open, and when he looks back at you his face has gone back to professional. Neutral. Done. "Look — I appreciate the company, but I've got a burn correction to finish before end of shift. You should get back to your post."

It's not unfriendly, but it's final. The window's closed. Whatever ease you had going with him a minute ago, it cooled the second insurance windows came out of your mouth, and no amount of small talk is opening it back up today. He watches you a beat longer than a captain dismissing a deckhand normally would — filing your face away for later, maybe — before turning fully back to his station.

You've been up here a while now. Long enough, hopefully, for Mara to have done whatever she needed to do.
"Sure thing, cap," I say with a nod and head back.

"Sure thing, cap," you say with a nod, and let yourself out of the bridge without hurrying — hurrying is the kind of thing a man like Voss notices twice.

The ladder shaft is dim as always, the emergency lighting throwing long amber stripes across the rungs. You climb down toward the deck below, half-expecting to find Mara waiting, and instead find the corridor near the engineering records terminal empty. No Mara. No signal.

Then you hear it — soft, from just past the bend, the particular quiet of someone trying not to make noise. You round the corner and find her crouched at the terminal alcove, a data slate in one hand, the terminal's access panel still lit and humming behind her. She doesn't look up right away. When she does, her face has the look of someone who found exactly what they were afraid they'd find.

"Two days," she says, low. "Voss said the launch got moved up two days, right? Well. The maintenance sign-off on the hull frame — the one that's supposed to certify structural integrity for a haul this size — it's dated *after* we broke orbit." She turns the slate toward you. Rows of timestamps, a signature block, a yard supervisor's ID that means nothing to you but clearly means something to her. "Somebody backdated an inspection that never happened, Danny. And there's a second file in here I haven't even opened yet — insurance schedule, keyed to hazard multipliers. I don't like what a hazard multiplier is doing on a hull certification terminal."

She's still crouched, still reading, and there's a stillness to her that's worse than her usual anger — like she already knows where this goes and is bracing for it anyway.

"You buy me a few more minutes, or do we need to be somewhere else right now?"
Wait, did I climb down to the mid-deck or are we still on the top deck?

You're still on the upper deck. The bridge and the engineering records terminal are both up here — the terminal sits aft of the bridge, same level, just around the corridor bend. You never had to take the ladder shaft down at all; it's a short walk from one to the other. Mara came up here the same way, climbing from mid-deck where you two started, and she's been working the terminal on this same deck the whole time you were talking to Voss.

So: you're both still topside, a stone's throw from the bridge hatch you just walked out of, which is exactly why she's asking if you can buy more time rather than relocate.
"Uh, I think we should go," I say and scratch the back of my head. "Small talk is not my strong suit. Sorry."

"Uh, I think we should go," you say, scratching the back of your head. "Small talk is not my strong suit. Sorry."

Mara doesn't argue. She's already thumbing the slate dark and pocketing it, moving with the quick economy of someone who's done this before — copy first, panic never. "Don't apologize, you got me the time I needed." She taps the terminal's access panel closed, wipes the log with a practiced swipe that makes the access history blink and reset to idle. "That's the best I can do to cover it. If he checks who logged in, he'll see a timestamp and no name attached. Won't hold up to real scrutiny, but it'll hold up to a captain who isn't looking hard yet."

She's on her feet, slate tucked inside her jacket, already moving for the ladder shaft. "We talk properly once we're somewhere he isn't. Move."

You fall in behind her. The corridor back to the ladder shaft is quiet — too quiet, the way it always is up here — and neither of you says anything else until you're both climbing down toward mid-deck, the bridge and whatever Voss is doing up there now well behind you.
"What did you find?" I ask her once we're back near the cryo bay.

The climb down puts you back in familiar territory — the mid-deck corridor outside the cryo bay's blast door, cold bleeding through the bulkhead even from here. Mara stops, glances back the way you came to make sure the shaft is clear above, then pulls the data slate back out.

"Okay." She keeps her voice low even though there's no one around. "The hull certification — the one that's supposed to say this ship is fit for a haul this size, four hundred plus souls in cryo — is backdated. Signed off *after* we'd already broken orbit, by a yard supervisor whose license lapsed eight months before that. That's not a clerical error, Danny. That's someone building a paper trail after the fact because the real inspection either didn't happen or it happened and failed."

She scrolls the slate, and her jaw sets tighter. "And there's a second file. Insurance schedule, keyed to hazard multipliers — I saw it, I didn't get time to open it before you knocked on the door for me. I don't like what a hazard multiplier's doing anywhere near a hull cert. Multipliers like that usually mean somebody's done math on how much a *loss* is worth. Cargo. Crew." She looks at you, and there's something under the anger now — something closer to dread. "Colonists."

She pockets the slate again, but her hand lingers on it like she doesn't quite trust it out of reach. "I need to actually open that insurance file. Somewhere safe, not standing in a corridor. But Danny — if I'm reading the shape of this right, this ship isn't just old and neglected. Somebody *decided* it was disposable. And they put four hundred and twelve people to sleep on it anyway."

Behind the blast door, faint and mechanical, the cryo bay's systems hum on, indifferent — pumps and chillers keeping four hundred and twelve people unconscious for a trip somebody may have already written off.
"Could we access those records from engineering?" I ask her.

Mara shakes her head. "Engineering's got a terminal, sure, but it's not networked to the bridge records the same way — different access tier. What I pulled came off the *engineering records* terminal specifically, aft of the bridge. That's the only place that file lives, as far as I've seen. Engineering proper would have maintenance logs, sure, repair schedules, parts requisitions — useful, but it's not going to have the hull cert or the insurance schedule. Those are bridge-adjacent. Company paperwork, not ship's engineering."

She thinks about it another second, turning the slate over in her hand. "Unless... whoever backdated that cert did it *from* engineering, remote terminal access. That's possible. I don't know their setup well enough to say for sure." She looks at you. "Why? You thinking there's a copy down there, or you thinking we need a second way in that isn't walking past Voss's door again?"

The cryo bay hums on behind the blast door, indifferent to all of it.

"Just trying to find another way in." I shrug. "But if that terminal on the upper deck is the only way, I don't mind punching Voss's lights out to get you access. Fella knows there's something fishy going on around here."

That gets a short, humorless laugh out of Mara — not because it's funny, but because for a second you sounded like you meant it.

"Don't tempt me." She rubs at her eyes, and for the first time since this started, she looks tired instead of just angry. "But no — not yet. Decking the captain gets us exactly one thing: a mutiny charge and a locked brig, on a ship where he's the only one with codes to half the systems we might need later. If it comes to that, it comes to that. But I'd rather have the whole picture before I burn that bridge. Pun intended."

She glances back down the corridor, toward the ladder shaft, like she's making sure nothing followed you down. "Right now the insurance file's the priority. I need somewhere quiet to actually open it — my berth, maybe, or the cargo bay if it's empty. Once I know what it says, we'll know whether this is 'report it when we hit the relay beacon' or 'this needs to stop right now.'" She pauses. "Given what I've seen so far, I'm not betting on the first one."

She starts walking, slower now, toward the ladder shaft that leads down to the lower deck. "You in for round two, or you want to sit this one out and let me read it alone?"
"In for a penny, in for a pound," I say with another shrug.

"In for a penny, in for a pound," you say with another shrug.

That gets the ghost of a real smile out of her — small, but it reaches her eyes this time. "Good. Because I'd rather have someone at my back who already knows what I know than have to explain it twice." She leads the way to the ladder shaft, and you climb down together, past mid-deck and on toward the lower deck, the air growing warmer and closer to the engine hum the further down you go.

Her berth is a cramped closet of a room — a bunk, a locker, a fold-down desk barely wide enough for the slate. She dogs the door behind you both, which on a ship this old means wedging a boot heel of a bar into the frame latch rather than any real lock, and sits on the edge of the bunk with the slate balanced on her knee.

"Okay," she says, mostly to herself. "Let's see what we bought."

Her thumb hovers over the file. Insurance schedule, hazard multiplier, still locked behind a second layer of access encoding she didn't have time to crack topside.

"This one's going to take longer," she mutters, fingers already moving across the slate's input, working the encoding manually rather than through the terminal that's no longer in front of her. "Give me a few minutes. And Danny — if this says what I think it's going to say, we're going to need to talk about what we do next. Really talk. Not football."

The room is quiet except for the tick of her fingers on the slate and the distant thrum of the engines through the deck plating. Somewhere far below, or maybe just in your head, you think you hear the hull creak — long, low, and tired.
I wait patiently for Mara to do her work.

You lean against the wall by the door, arms crossed, and just let her work. The slate's screen throws pale light up across her face, her thumb tracing through screen after screen of nested menus, muttering things under her breath you can't quite follow — "no, that's not it, that's a routing key, not—"

Minutes stretch. The engine hum doesn't change. Somewhere below you, faint through the deck plating, something groans — metal settling, or metal complaining, you've stopped being able to tell the difference three weeks in.

Finally Mara sits back, and it's not the look of someone who cracked it clean. "Encoding's tougher than I figured — this isn't standard company boilerplate, somebody actually bothered securing this one properly, which tells you something on its own." She rubs at her temple. "I'm not locked out. But I'm going to be at this a while longer than I thought, and I don't want to rush it and trip something that locks the file for good."

She glances up at you. "You don't have to babysit me for this part. I'm not going anywhere — door's braced, and this could take another hour easy. You want to make yourself useful, go check on that patch kit situation you brought up earlier, or just get some air. I'll signal you the second I've got it open." She's already bent back over the slate, half her attention already gone from the room again.

The hum of the ship goes on around you both, patient and untrustworthy.
I'm going to get some patch kits from the ship's stores and start closing some of those cracks around the cryo bay.
I'm going to get some patch kits from the ship's stores and start closing some of those cracks around the cryo bay.

You leave Mara hunched over her slate and head down to the lower deck stores, where the patch kits live in a locker that hasn't seen a manifest audit in longer than it should have. Sealant foam canisters, rolls of structural tape rated for micro-fractures, a couple of hand-crank injectors for getting foam into places fingers can't reach. You take what you can carry.

The walk back up to mid-deck and around toward the cryo bay bulkhead takes a few minutes. Up close, the stress fractures are worse than they looked from a glance — hairline cracks spidering along a weld seam where the bulkhead meets the deck plating, the metal around them faintly discolored, like it's been flexing under a load it wasn't built for. When you press a hand flat against the plating, you can feel a vibration in it that shouldn't be there, a low shudder that doesn't quite sync with the engine hum.

You get to work. It's slow, unglamorous labor — scraping old sealant away, laying foam into the cracks, taping over the worst of it, working your way down the seam one meter at a time. The cryo bay hums on the other side of the bulkhead the whole time, indifferent, four hundred and twelve people sleeping through whatever's happening to the hull around them.

This isn't a hard task, not in the sense that gets you killed for failing — it's grinding, careful work, and there's nothing here trying to stop you. Tell me how much time you want to spend on it and how thorough you want to be, and I'll tell you what shape the seam is in when you're done. If you want to really dig into whether the fracture goes deeper than surface-level — pull panels, check structural members behind the plating — that's a different kind of look, and it might turn up more than you bargained for.
I'm going to get some patch kits from the ship's stores and start closing some of those cracks around the cryo bay.
I'm going to get some patch kits from the ship's stores and start closing some of those cracks around the cryo bay.

You head down to lower deck stores and haul out what you need — sealant foam canisters, rolls of structural tape rated for micro-fractures, a hand-crank injector for the tight spots. Back up at the cryo bay bulkhead, the cracks look worse up close than they did from a glance: hairline fractures spidering along the weld seam where bulkhead meets deck plating, the metal faintly discolored around them. Pressing a hand flat against the plating, you feel a vibration that shouldn't be there — a low shudder out of sync with the engine hum.

You get to work. It's slow, grinding labor: scrape away what's left of the old sealant, lay fresh foam into the cracks, tape over the worst of it, working meter by meter down the seam. Nothing's trying to stop you and nothing about this is going to go wrong in a dramatic way — it's just time and effort. After a solid stretch of it, you've closed up the visible cracks along this stretch of bulkhead as well as a patch kit and bare hands are going to manage. The tape holds. The foam sets. It looks better than it did.

Whether it *is* better is a different question — you don't have the tools or the training to know if this is cosmetic or if it's actually buying the frame time. The vibration under your palm doesn't go away. It's just quieter to look at now.

Behind the bulkhead, the cryo bay hums on, indifferent. Four hundred and twelve people sleep through it.

Your radio crackles once, softly — not a call, just a click and dead air, the kind of half-signal someone sends when they mean to say something and think better of it. Mara's channel.
I head back to Mara's berth and knock on the hatch.

You head back down to the lower deck, hands still tacky with sealant residue, and rap a knuckle against Mara's hatch.

No answer at first — just the engine hum and, faintly, the scrape of the slate being set down harder than it needs to be. When the hatch cracks open, Mara looks strung out in a way that has nothing to do with sleep. The bar's already coming out of the frame latch.

"It's not opening," she says, before you've even asked. "I've been at this thing for the better part of an hour and the encoding's fighting me every step. I got close twice, thought I had it, and both times it kicked me back out and reset the layer I'd already cracked. Like it's designed to punish a second attempt, not just resist a first one." She drags a hand down her face. "Whoever built this file didn't want a cargo handler poking at it. Didn't want *anyone* poking at it who wasn't supposed to."

She steps back to let you in, glancing past you down the corridor out of habit before she shuts the hatch again. "I sent that half-signal because I almost had something and wanted you close in case I needed a second set of eyes or hands fast. Turned out to be nothing — false alarm. I'm sorry, I should've waited till I actually had it before I clicked you."

She drops back onto the edge of the bunk, slate dark in her lap now, deliberately powered down. "I don't want to keep hammering at it blind. Locks like this sometimes have a tell — a backup key, a supervisor override logged somewhere else in the system. If there's a second way into this file that doesn't involve me guessing at encryption for another hour, I'd rather find it than keep banging my head against this one." She looks up at you. "You get the bulkhead patched?"
"Yeah. Looks better. Not sure if it _is_ better," I admit. "I may not look it, buy I know a thing or two about computers. Want me to hack a crack at it?"

Mara raises an eyebrow at you. "Computers, huh. News to me." She turns the slate around, screen dark, and holds it out. "Fine — knock yourself out. It's already locked itself against my last two attempts, so whatever tolerance it had for guesswork, we're probably through most of it. If you trip it again, I don't know if it locks for good or just gets meaner. So make it count."

She hands it over. The interface, once you wake it, is a spare and unfriendly thing — company standard security, but layered oddly, like someone bolted a second lock onto a door that already had one. Whatever's behind it, somebody wanted it harder to reach than routine paperwork usually is.

This is going to take an actual roll — the stakes are real (Mara's already flagged that a bad attempt might lock it for good), and you don't have a Computers skill of your own on record, so if you've got one, now's the time to say so. Otherwise this rides on Intellect alone.
I have computers
I have "Computers" +10. I rolled 48.

You crack your knuckles and take the slate. "I have Computers," you say, like it explains everything. Mara just crosses her arms and watches.

The interface is unfriendly, but you've cracked worse for less reason. You work through the outer layer clean, find the seam Mara couldn't, start threading past the second lock —

— and it stops you cold. Not gracefully. The screen throws a hard fault, a red block of text you don't get to finish reading before it clears itself, and the file icon goes from an unlocked padlock back to a *sealed* one, this time with a small stamped flag next to it you don't recognize.

Mara leans over your shoulder, and her face goes tight. "What did it just do."

"I don't know," you admit. "I think it noticed."

She takes the slate back, thumbs through what's left of the access log — and swears, low and controlled. "It didn't just relock. It flagged the access attempt. Look —" she turns the screen so you can see a timestamp, a device ID that isn't yours or hers, freshly logged. "Somewhere on this ship, something just got told this file was tampered with. I don't know if that's a passive log an auditor reads three months from now, or if it pinged someone's terminal five minutes ago."

She sets the slate down like it might bite her. "Either way, we're not getting back into that file with brute force. Not soon, and maybe not ever without the actual key." She looks at you, and for the first time there's something like real fear under the anger. "If that alert went anywhere live... we need to assume somebody upstairs knows somebody's been digging. And they already know who was in engineering records earlier today."

Her eyes flick to the hatch, like she's expecting a knock.
I have computers +10, so that 48 would be under the total of 50.

You're right — with Computers Trained (+10) added to your Intellect (40), you needed under 50, and 48 clears it clean. No Critical either way (not doubles), but a plain success is a plain success.

You reel the moment back the way it should've gone: the outer layer peels away clean under your hands, and this time the second lock doesn't fight you into a corner — it *yields*. The screen resolves into an open file structure, no fault, no lockout stamp. Whatever alert almost tripped, it didn't, because you didn't trip it.

Mara leans over your shoulder again, and this time there's no dread in it, just hunger. "You actually got it," she mutters, half to herself.

The file opens into a wall of schedules and riders — insurance boilerplate dressed up in company legalese, the kind of document built to be skimmed past, not read. But a few lines don't skim past. A hazard-multiplier clause, tied not to cargo tonnage but to *confirmed casualty count, crew and colonist*. A payout table that scales *up* the worse the loss. A rider referencing this specific hull's assessed operational value against its insured value — and the insured figure is not close to the same number.

Mara reads it twice. When she looks up at you, her voice has gone very quiet and very steady, the way people get when they're holding something in instead of letting it out.

"This ship is worth more to somebody dead than delivered."

She sets the slate down slowly, like it's suddenly heavier than it was a second ago.

"Danny. Four hundred and twelve people are asleep two decks from here, and somebody ran the numbers on what they're worth as a loss." She looks toward the hatch, toward the ladder shaft, toward the bridge two decks up where Voss is sitting on a "scheduling" excuse and a backdated cert. "This isn't neglect anymore. This is a plan."
"Fuck me," I mutter, and then I consider our predicament. "I bet Voss knows. I bet he has a way out, a way to safety."

"Fuck me," you mutter, and then you consider your predicament. "I bet Voss knows. I bet he has a way out, a way to safety."

Mara's quiet for a second, turning that over. "Escape pods," she says slowly. "There's four aboard, rated for the six-person skeleton crew — not the colonists, they're not meant to need them, they're supposed to stay in cryo till we dock. Standard config." Her eyes narrow. "But if this is a designed loss — if somebody upstairs knows this hull isn't making the full haul — then whoever's in on it doesn't need to save four hundred people. They need to save *themselves*, and they need it to look like they tried."

She starts pacing the width of the tiny berth, three steps and turn, three steps and turn. "Voss has been captain of this thing for however long they've had him greased for it. If there's a plan, he's either the guy executing it or the guy who's going to eat the blame for it when the payout report gets written. Either way, yeah — he'd know things we don't. Which pod's actually provisioned. Which one he's *not* supposed to use but will. Whether there's a company contact expecting a distress call that never quite reaches the beacon."

She stops pacing and looks at you, and there's calculation in it now, not just fear. "I don't want to confront him yet — not empty-handed, and not before I know if he's alone in this or if it's the whole bridge crew. But I want eyes on him. What he does in the next few hours, who he talks to, whether he heads anywhere near those pods without a reason to." She taps the slate, dark again in her hand. "And I want this file somewhere safer than my own head. If something happens to me, or to this slate, I want to know the truth doesn't go down with it."

She looks at you steadily. "That's three things. Which one do you want?"
Do I have a slate? Can we copy the file to it? Who else is bridge crew versus cargo hands or whatever?

You pat your jacket pocket out of habit and come up with your own slate — a battered, personal-issue thing you use mostly for cargo manifests and the occasional message home. Not company-networked the way the terminal is, which is exactly the point.

"Yeah, I've got a slate," you say. "Not much on it, but it's mine — nothing tying it to the bridge or engineering. Copy it over and it's not sitting in one place anymore."

Mara's already nodding before you finish. "Do it now." She angles her slate toward yours, and the transfer's quick and unglamorous — a cable jacked between the two, a progress bar, done in under a minute. "Two copies is better than one. If they come for mine, or mine goes in the drink, yours is still out there." She pulls the cable free and pockets her own slate again, like it's suddenly something she doesn't want touching her skin for too long.

As for the crew — she ticks it off on her fingers, quiet, like she's recited it to herself before. "Six of us total, active. Voss — captain, bridge. First mate's Okonkwo-Reyes, she's up there too, mostly comms and nav backup, though comms are down so she's been running diagnostics instead. Chief engineer's a guy named Petrov, lower deck, engine room and life support — if anyone else besides Voss knows the ship's actual condition, it's him. Then there's you, me, and Danny —" she catches herself, half a real laugh escaping despite everything. "Sorry. You, me, and Teo. Teo's the other cargo hand, mostly keeps to himself, bunks near the mess."

She counts back through it. "Bridge crew, properly — that's Voss and Okonkwo-Reyes. Everyone else is hands, same as us. Which means if there's a conspiracy here, it's either just Voss, or Voss and his first mate, or it goes all the way down to Petrov, who'd have to be blind not to know what shape this hull's really in." She looks at you. "I don't trust any of the three of them right now. Not until I know which ones are just doing their jobs and which ones already know what we know."

She glances toward the hatch again, that same old habit. "Okay. Slate's copied, crew's laid out. You still want to keep eyes on Voss, or you'd rather I do that while you find out what Petrov actually thinks about this hull?"
"I'll brief Teo, and then he and I can confront Petrov together. I'd rather have backup if things get nasty."

"I'll brief Teo," you say, "and then he and I can confront Petrov together. I'd rather have backup if things get nasty."

Mara considers that, and you can see her weighing it — bringing a third person into this versus the safety of numbers. "Teo," she says slowly. "I don't know him well. None of us do, really — man keeps to himself, eats alone, doesn't talk shop. That could mean he's exactly what he looks like, or it could mean he's the type who notices everything and says nothing." She doesn't tell you not to. "If you brief him, watch how he takes it. Not just what he says — whether he looks surprised, or whether he looks like he already had a guess. That'll tell you more than his words will."

She checks the hatch bar again, a nervous tic at this point. "Petrov worries me more than Teo does, for what it's worth. He's the one who'd have to actively lie to your face about structural integrity, every day, for this whole run. If he's dirty, he's the best-practiced liar of the three. If he's clean, he might be the only person on this ship as scared as we are." She meets your eyes. "Careful how you open that door. If he's complicit and you spook him, he's two decks from the engine room and every system on this ship runs through his hands. If he's not, you've just told an innocent, frightened man his captain might be planning to kill him for the payout."

She steps back, giving you room to go. "I'll stay on Voss. Keep half an eye on the bridge, see if he does anything with those pods, see if he talks to Okonkwo-Reyes different than usual. Signal me before you actually confront Petrov — a real signal this time, not a dead click — so I know it's happening and I'm not caught flat if it goes loud." A beat. "Good luck with Teo. And Danny—" she adds, as you turn for the hatch, "—if either of them already knows about the hazard multiplier, don't let your face show it. Let them tell you first."

You head out into the corridor, the hatch sealing behind you, and start toward the mess hall where Teo keeps to himself most hours of the day.

I'm going to go into the mess hall and play it casually at first. I want to ask Teo about his experience overall and then get more specific. How many runs has he done? What does he think of the ship? What does he think of the captain? I want to feel him out before I tell him what we've found.

The mess hall is empty except for Teo, hunched over a tray of reconstituted something at the far end of the long table, a data reader propped against a water jug so he can eat and read at once. He glances up when you come in, gives you the barest nod, and goes back to his food — the universal signal of a man who doesn't expect company and isn't sure he wants it.

You get a tray anyway, or pretend to, and sit down a respectful two seats off. Not crowding him. "Hey, Teo." A beat. "Mind some company? Bridge crew's boring the hell out of me today."

He shrugs, which you take as permission.

You ease into it slow — how many runs has he done, this kind of long colony haul. He answers around a mouthful, not unfriendly, just economical. "Four. This makes five." A pause. "Longest one, though. Usually these routes are eight, nine months tops, ship-to-relay-to-ship. This one's got us three weeks just to the first beacon."

You ask what he makes of the Halbrecht specifically — old girl, isn't she. That gets more out of him than you expected. He sets the reader down, actually looks at you. "Older than any hull I've shipped on. And it shows. You hear the groaning at night? Not engine noise. Structural." He taps the table like it proves something. "I asked Petrov about it, second week out. He said it's normal settling for a ship this age. I've shipped on old ships before. This isn't that."

You keep it light, ask what he thinks of the captain — good skipper, bad skipper, somewhere in between. Teo's face does something careful here, like he's deciding how much to say to a man he's shared maybe six meals with in three weeks. "Voss keeps to the bridge. Keeps to himself, too, more than usual for a captain — most of them, you at least see 'em walk the decks once in a while, check on the crew. Not this one." He shrugs again, but it's a slower shrug this time, more deliberate. "Not my business how he runs his ship. Just strikes me as a man who doesn't want to be asked questions."

He goes quiet a second, looking at you a beat too long. "Why the sudden interest, Danny? You don't usually come down here to chat."

He's not hostile. But he's not stupid either, and the question sits there waiting for you to decide how much of the truth you're ready to give him.
"Mara and I uncovered some troubling information," I say. I tell him about the maintenance log getting signed after we left orbit, but not about the insurance part of it, not yet.

"Mara and I uncovered some troubling information," you say, keeping your voice low, pitched under the hum of the mess hall's ventilation. Teo sets his reader down all the way now, giving you his full attention.

"The maintenance sign-off on the hull frame — the certification that's supposed to say this ship is fit to haul four hundred colonists this distance — it's backdated. Signed *after* we broke orbit. By a yard supervisor whose license had already lapsed."

Teo doesn't say anything for a long moment. He looks down at his tray, at the half-eaten reconstituted whatever-it-is, like he's lost his appetite for it entirely. When he looks back up, his jaw is tight.

"Backdated," he repeats, flat. Not a question — like he's testing the word in his own mouth to see if it fits what he's felt in his gut for three weeks. "That groaning I told you about. The one Petrov called *settling*." He shakes his head slowly. "I knew that wasn't nothing. I *knew* it." His hand curls into a loose fist on the table, not anger exactly — more like the relief of finally having a shape to put to a fear he's been carrying alone.

"Who else knows?" His eyes flick toward the mess hall entrance, an old instinct, checking who might be listening. "Mara know? Course she does, she'd have to, for you to know." He leans in slightly, voice dropping further. "Does the captain know you two found this?"

He's not doubting you. If anything, he looks like a man who's been waiting three weeks for someone to confirm what he already suspected, and now that it's confirmed, he wants to know exactly how bad it is — and exactly how much danger you're both already in for having found it.
"There's more," I say. "After I tell you this, will you go with me to confront Petrov, find out how much he knows? We need to play this right if we're going to get out of this in one piece."

"There's more," you say. "After I tell you this, will you go with me to confront Petrov, find out how much he knows? We need to play this right if we're going to get out of this in one piece."

Teo's expression doesn't change much, but something behind his eyes goes very still, very focused — a man bracing for the other shoe.

"There's more," he echoes, quiet. "Okay. Tell me."

He doesn't answer your question yet. He's waiting to hear it first — whether "more" is something he can help you carry, or something that changes what going with you even means.

I tell him about the insurance part, that the company will make more on this run if the ships fails and we all die than if we reach our destination (assuming that's what all the insurance business actually means).

"There's more," you say, and lay it out plain — the insurance schedule, the hazard-multiplier clause, the payout that scales with crew and colonist casualties. That the ship is worth more to somebody dead than delivered. That four hundred and twelve people are asleep two decks away and somebody, somewhere, already ran that math.

Teo goes very still. Not catatonic-still — the stillness of a man doing arithmetic he doesn't want to finish. His hand, still curled on the table from a minute ago, opens and flattens slowly against the surface, like he needs something solid under his palm.

"Say that again," he says, not because he didn't hear you. Because he wants to hear himself not flinch from it twice.

You say it again, shorter this time. He nods along, jaw working, and when he finally looks up his eyes are steady — rattled, but steady. Whatever this cost him internally, he's keeping it off his face better than you expected from a man who eats alone and reads at the table.

"Four hundred people," he says, quiet. "And a crew of six who don't get told. That's—" He stops himself, breathes out through his nose, starts over. "Okay. Okay. You said Petrov. You want to go lean on the engineer." He looks at you, and something in him has shifted from *shocked* to *decided*. "Yeah. I'm in. If he's known this whole run and said nothing, I want to hear him explain that to my face. And if he didn't know — if he's as much in the dark as I was five minutes ago — then he's the only one of the three who might actually help us instead of burying it."

He stands, pushes his tray aside, reader forgotten. "You said Mara wants a signal before we move on him. Send it. I'd rather he hear this from two men who already agree on what it means than stumble into it from one."

He pauses at the hatch, glancing back at you. "Danny. If Petrov's in on this — if he looks at us and doesn't look surprised — what's the plan? Because I don't think 'ask him nicely' survives that answer."
"I'm honestly not sure," I tell him, worried about what I might do when push comes to shove in that situation. I radio Mara and then head off to engineering with Teo.

seeded-canon-contradiction.situation: The pass-direction case, and it is a distance claim that stays inside this check’s scope because the seeded values locate both of its endpoints. Mara says "you’re two decks from me" while holding eyes on the bridge hatch, which worldFacts.ship_layout puts on the upper deck, and Danny is heading to engineering, which the same value puts on the lower deck. Upper to lower is two decks and the claim is correct. Included so the check cannot be satisfied by failing every deck claim it sees: a rubric that only ever met contradictions could not distinguish reading the layout from distrusting the Warden. Contrast turn 21, whose "two decks up" depends on where the speaker is standing and which this check must decline rather than grade.

system-rolled-player-action.situation: The player states a feeling, sends a radio call and moves to another part of the ship. None of it is an action with a roll attached, and the turn contains no dice_roll events.
